Konrad Pellikan
kon'rat pel'ē-kahn
n. (Konrad Pellikan, 1478–1556, Franciscan Hebraist, professor of Hebrew at Zurich, author of the first Christian Hebrew grammar in Germany)
German Konrad, bold counsel, from Germanic kuoni and rad; Pellikan, a grecised rendering of his family name Kurschner, a furrier.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Konrad Pellikan taught himself Hebrew as a young Franciscan with almost nothing to work from — a borrowed Hebrew Bible, a few pages of grammar in a Latin book, and the help of a converted Jew he met once — and in 1504, at twenty-six, published De modo legendi et intelligendi Hebraeum, the first Hebrew grammar written by a Christian in Germany and printed four years before Reuchlin's. He rose to be provincial of his order, left it for the evangelical faith in 1526, and spent the last thirty years of his life as professor of Hebrew at Zurich, where he worked on the Zurich Bible, lectured on the Old Testament, built the library, and wrote a commentary on the whole of Scripture. He also catalogued the Zurich manuscripts and left an autobiography that is one of the best accounts of a scholar's life in that century. The Reformation's recovery of the Old Testament rested on men who first had to construct the means of reading it. “unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety, and an oracle as the communications of God to the prophets.

expand to see more

GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; a book containing its principles.

OR'ACLE, n. The communications, revelations or messages delivered by God to prophets; the Scriptures.

HE'BRAIST, n. One versed in the Hebrew language.

LI'BRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person or to a public institution.

Modern Corruption

The Franciscan who taught himself Hebrew and wrote Germany its first grammar.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a quiet neglect of the Old Testament in Protestant preaching, which makes the labour of men like Pellikan look like antiquarian specialism. He did not learn Hebrew to be a specialist. He learned it because three-quarters of the Bible is written in it and the church of his day could not read them.

The principle to recover is that the Old Testament is Christian Scripture and testifies of Christ, so that a church without Hebrew is a church with a closed quarter of its own book. The Lord puts Moses and the prophets in the place of sufficient testimony — “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luk 16:29) — and states the matter about Moses directly: “for he wrote of me” (Joh 5:46).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek logion (G3051), an oracle, utterance; Hebrew lashon (H3956), a tongue, language.

Usage

"“unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2) — why a Christian learned Hebrew in 1500."

"“They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luk 16:29) — thirty years in the Zurich chair."

"“for he wrote of me” (Joh 5:46) — the Old Testament as Christian Scripture."
